p7-1.a: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components; it keeps a virtual DOM and updates only what changed when state changes. Declarative: you describe the UI for a given state.
p7-1.qa: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React reconciles changes efficiently (virtual DOM diffing) to update only what changed in the real DOM.
i: React 18 introduced concurrent rendering, automatic batching and transitions.
React 19 (Dec 2024): Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic, the use() hook, ref as a prop, and Server Components support.
React Compiler (stable 2025) auto-memoises components, reducing manual useMemo/useCallback.
One-way data flow: props down, events up.
f: What is reconciliation?
React compares the new element tree with the previous one and applies minimal DOM changes.
Why keys in lists?
Stable keys let React match items between renders and keep state correct.

p7-2.a: A component is a function (or class) that returns UI; an element is the plain object it returns describing what to render, for example `<Button />` creates an element of the Button component.
p7-2.qa: A component is a function (or class) that returns UI; an element is the plain object it returns describing what to render. <Button /> creates an element of type Button; React calls the component to get more elements until it reaches DOM elements.
i: Elements are immutable descriptions; cheap to create.
JSX compiles to jsx() calls (new JSX transform).
An element is a plain object describing UI ({type, props}); a component is a function that returns elements.
JSX <Button/> compiles to a jsx() call that creates an element.
f: Is JSX required?
No, but it's the standard and compiles to function calls.
What is a fragment?
<>...</> groups elements without adding a DOM node.

p7-3.a: Functional: plain functions using hooks for state and effects; less code, easier reuse with custom hooks; the modern standard.|Class: extend React.Component with this.state and lifecycle methods; still needed only for error boundaries.
p7-3.qa: Functional components are plain functions using hooks for state and effects: less code, easier reuse through custom hooks, and the modern standard. Class components extend React.Component with this.state and lifecycle methods; they're still supported but only needed for error boundaries today.
i: Hooks rules: call at top level, only in components or custom hooks.
Lifecycle mapping: componentDidMount/Update/WillUnmount ≈ useEffect with cleanup.
Hooks replaced most class lifecycle methods; error boundaries are the main case still needing a class.
Function components are simpler, easier to test and work with concurrent features.
f: Why are error boundaries still classes?
They rely on componentDidCatch/getDerivedStateFromError, which have no hook equivalent.
Can you mix both?
Yes, in the same app.

p7-4.a: Props: read-only inputs passed from parent to child.|State: data owned by a component that changes over time (useState) and triggers re-render.|Props flow down and are controlled by the parent; state is local and controlled by the component.
p7-4.qa: Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child; state is data owned by a component that changes over time (useState) and triggers a re-render. Props flow down and are controlled by the parent; state is local and changed by the component itself, often passed down as props.
i: Lift state up to the nearest common parent when siblings need it.
State updates are asynchronous and batched; use functional updates (setCount(c => c + 1)).
Never mutate state directly; create new objects or arrays.
State updates are asynchronous and batched (automatic batching in React 18+).
f: Why functional updates?
They use the latest state when updates are batched.
Derived state?
Compute it during render instead of storing it.

p7-5.a: The second argument of useEffect, useMemo and useCallback: the hook re-runs when any listed value changes.|Empty array: the effect runs once after the first render (and cleans up on unmount). No array: runs after every render.
p7-5.qa: The dependency array is the second argument of useEffect, useMemo and useCallback: the hook re-runs when any listed value changes (compared with Object.is). An empty array runs the effect once after the first render (and cleanup on unmount); no array runs it after every render.
i: In development StrictMode, effects run twice on mount to reveal missing cleanups.
The ESLint react-hooks/exhaustive-deps rule catches missing dependencies.
Objects created during render change every time, causing repeated effects.
f: Why does my effect run twice in development?
StrictMode intentionally double-invokes to find bugs.
What's a stale closure?
An effect using old values because dependencies were omitted.

p7-6.a: useMemo caches a computed value between renders until dependencies change.|useCallback caches a function reference, so memoised children do not re-render because of a new function.|useCallback(fn, deps) equals useMemo(() => fn, deps).
p7-6.qa: useMemo caches a computed value between renders until dependencies change; useCallback caches a function reference so memoised children (React.memo) don't re-render because of a new function prop. useCallback(fn, deps) equals useMemo(() => fn, deps).
i: Only use them when profiling shows a benefit or for referential stability in dependencies.
React Compiler can make most manual memoisation unnecessary.
useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function identity (useCallback(fn) is useMemo(() => fn)).
React Compiler (stable 2025) can memoize automatically, reducing manual use.
f: Does useMemo guarantee caching?
No, React may discard cached values; treat it as an optimisation.
When does useCallback help?
When passing callbacks to memoised children or as effect dependencies.

p7-7.a: Returns a mutable object whose .current persists across renders without causing a re-render; used for DOM references (focus an input) and for values such as timers or previous values.
p7-7.qa: useRef returns a mutable object whose .current persists across renders without causing a re-render. It's used for DOM references (focusing an input) and for values like timers, previous values or abort controllers.
i: React 19 allows ref as a regular prop for function components (forwardRef no longer needed).
Don't read or write ref.current during render for values that affect output.
Changing ref.current doesn't re-render; useful for DOM nodes, timers and previous values.
f: useRef vs useState?
Changing a ref doesn't re-render; changing state does.
What is forwardRef for?
Passing refs to child components (unnecessary in React 19).

p7-8.a: Context passes values (theme, current user, locale) down the tree without prop drilling.|Context is fine for low-frequency global values; Redux (Toolkit) adds a predictable store, middleware, devtools and selective subscriptions for large, frequently changing state. For server data, React Query is often better than both.
p7-8.qa: Context passes values (theme, current user, locale) down the tree without prop drilling. It's fine for low-frequency global values; Redux Toolkit adds a predictable store, devtools and middleware for complex shared state, and libraries like Zustand are lighter alternatives. Server data is best handled by React Query.
i: Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes; split contexts and memoise values.
Redux Toolkit with RTK Query reduces boilerplate.
Context passes values without prop drilling; every consumer re-renders when the value changes.
Redux Toolkit adds a store with selectors, devtools and middleware; use it for complex shared state.
f: Is Context a state manager?
It's a transport mechanism; state still lives in useState/useReducer.
When choose Redux?
Large apps with complex shared client state and many updates.

p7-9.a: A typed API client (fetch or axios) with interceptors for tokens and errors; React Query or a custom hook to fetch, cache and retry.|Show a loading indicator, an error message with retry, and an empty state; cancel requests on unmount with AbortController.
p7-9.qa: I use a typed API client (fetch or axios) with interceptors for tokens and errors, and React Query (TanStack Query) or a custom hook to fetch, cache and retry. The UI shows a loading indicator, an error message with retry, and an empty state, and maps ProblemDetails errors to user-friendly messages.
i: React Query handles caching, background refetch, deduplication and invalidation after mutations.
Abort requests on unmount or parameter change.
Suspense and error boundaries for declarative loading/error UI.
f: Why React Query over useEffect fetching?
It handles caching, races, retries and refetching for you.
How do you refresh after a mutation?
Invalidate the related query keys.

p7-10.a: Controlled: React state holds the input value (value + onChange), giving validation and formatting on every keystroke.|Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, read with a ref when needed; simpler and used by libraries like React Hook Form for performance.
p7-10.qa: In a controlled component React state holds the input value (value + onChange), giving validation and formatting on every keystroke. In an uncontrolled component the DOM holds the value, read with a ref or form submission, which is simpler and faster for big forms; React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance.
i: File inputs are always uncontrolled.
React 19 form actions work naturally with uncontrolled forms.
Controlled: value lives in React state; uncontrolled: DOM holds it and you read via refs.
React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance.
f: Which is better?
Controlled for dynamic validation; uncontrolled for performance and simplicity.
Warning "changing an uncontrolled input to controlled"?
The value went from undefined to defined; initialise state properly.

p7-11.a: A parent re-rendering re-renders its children; new object, array or function props each render; context values that change often; state kept too high in the tree. Fix with React.memo, useMemo/useCallback, splitting context and moving state down; measure with the Profiler first.
p7-11.qa: Causes are a parent re-rendering (children re-render by default), new object, array or function props each render, context values that change often, and state kept too high in the tree. Fixes: move state down, React.memo with stable props (useMemo/useCallback), split contexts, virtualise long lists, and measure with React DevTools Profiler.
i: Re-renders aren't always bad; only fix measured problems.
Keys: changing keys remount components.
Parent re-renders, new object/function props each render, and context value changes.
Profile with React DevTools before optimizing with memo.
f: How do you find unnecessary renders?
React DevTools Profiler "why did this render".
What does React.memo do?
Skips re-rendering if props are shallowly equal.

p7-12.a: Login through the SSO or OIDC provider (Authorization Code with PKCE); keep tokens in memory or HttpOnly cookies, not localStorage; an auth context exposes the user and roles.|Protected routes: a wrapper component that redirects unauthenticated users to login and checks roles. The API must still enforce authorisation.
p7-12.qa: Login through the SSO/OIDC provider (Authorization Code with PKCE), keep tokens in memory or HttpOnly cookies (BFF), not localStorage; an auth context exposes the user and roles; protected route components redirect unauthenticated users and hide unauthorised UI, while the API always enforces authorization.
i: Silent token renewal; handle 401 by re-authenticating.
MSAL or oidc-client-ts libraries.
Route guards only hide UI; real protection is on the API with token validation.
f: Is hiding UI enough?
No, the backend must enforce every permission.
Why not localStorage?
Any XSS can read it.

p7-13.a: React Hook Form (or Formik) for state and performance, with a schema validator (Zod or Yup) shared with types; show field errors, disable submit while saving, and map server validation errors (ProblemDetails) back to fields.
p7-13.qa: React Hook Form (or Formik) for state and performance, with a schema validator (Zod or Yup) whose types are shared with TypeScript; show field errors, disable submit while saving, and map server validation errors (ProblemDetails) back to fields.
i: zodResolver connects schema validation.
Server is still the source of truth for validation.
React Hook Form with Zod schemas for validation shared with types.
c:
const schema = z.object({ siteNumber: z.string().min(3), kitCount: z.number().int().positive() });
const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } = useForm({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) });
f: Why Zod?
One schema gives runtime validation and TypeScript types.
How do you show server errors?
setError on fields from the ProblemDetails errors dictionary.

p7-14.a: Feature-based folders (shipments/, sites/) with components, hooks, API calls and tests together; a shared library of reusable components; a typed API layer; routing with lazy-loaded features; consistent lint, formatting and testing rules.
p7-14.qa: Feature-based folders (shipments/, sites/) with components, hooks, API calls and tests together; a shared library of reusable UI components; a typed API layer (generated from OpenAPI); routing with lazy-loaded routes; global state kept minimal; and lint, format and test standards.
i: Code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense.
Storybook for component documentation.
Absolute imports and barrel files used carefully.
Feature-based folders (shipments/, imports/) with components, hooks and API clients together.
f: Why feature folders?
Related code changes together, making features easier to find and own.
How do you share components across apps?
An internal package or monorepo library.

p7-15.a: React: a focused UI library, flexible, large ecosystem, easy to adopt piece by piece, simpler learning curve.|Angular: a full framework with DI, routing, forms and RxJS built in, good for large teams wanting one opinionated way.|IRT has both; for new reusable components we used React for flexibility, while Angular modules remain where they already exist.
p7-15.qa: React is a focused UI library: flexible, large ecosystem, easy to adopt piece by piece and a simpler learning curve. Angular is a full framework with DI, routing, forms and RxJS built in, offering strong conventions for large teams. IRT uses both: Angular modules for older areas and React components for newer work.
i: Angular's recent signals and standalone components simplify it.
Choice depends on team skills and existing code.
React: flexible library, huge ecosystem, team experience; Angular: batteries-included framework with strong conventions.
Both are fine; choose on team skills and project needs.
f: Which would you choose for a new project?
Usually React with TypeScript, unless the team is strongly Angular.
What are Angular signals?
Reactive primitives for fine-grained change detection.

p7-16.a: var: function-scoped, hoisted and initialised as undefined, can be redeclared.|let: block-scoped, reassignable.|const: block-scoped, cannot be reassigned (the object it points to can still change). Default to const, use let when needed, avoid var.
p7-16.qa: var is function-scoped, hoisted and initialised as undefined, and can be redeclared; let is block-scoped and reassignable; const is block-scoped and can't be reassigned (but objects it points to can be mutated). Use const by default, let when reassigning, never var.
i: let/const are in the temporal dead zone before declaration.
Classic bug: var in loops with closures shares one variable.
var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined; let/const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone.
const prevents reassignment, not mutation of objects.
f: Is a const array immutable?
No, you can push to it; use Object.freeze for shallow immutability.
Why avoid var?
Function scoping and hoisting cause subtle bugs.

p7-17.a: Declarations are processed before code runs: function declarations are fully hoisted, var is hoisted as undefined, and let/const are hoisted but in the temporal dead zone until their line runs (accessing them throws).
p7-17.qa: Declarations are processed before code runs: function declarations are fully hoisted, var is hoisted as undefined, and let/const/class are hoisted but in the temporal dead zone, so accessing them early throws ReferenceError.
i: Function expressions and arrow functions assigned to variables follow variable rules.
Declarations are registered during the creation phase before code runs.
Function declarations are fully hoisted; function expressions assigned to var are hoisted as undefined.
let/const/class are hoisted but in the TDZ: access before declaration throws ReferenceError.
f: What prints console.log(x); var x = 5?
undefined.
And with let?
ReferenceError.

p7-18.a: A function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished, for example a counter factory or a debounce function keeping its timer.
p7-18.qa: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope finished, for example a counter factory or a debounce function keeping its timer. React hooks rely heavily on closures.
i: Stale closures in React effects come from capturing old state.
A function keeps access to variables from its outer scope even after the outer function returns.
Uses: private state, factories, React hooks capturing state (stale closures are a common bug).
f: Memory risk?
Closures keep captured objects alive as long as the function exists.
Same concept in C#?
Yes, lambdas capturing variables.

p7-19.a: A Promise represents a future value: pending, then fulfilled or rejected, handled with then/catch.|async/await is syntax over Promises that reads like synchronous code, with try/catch for errors; Promise.all still runs things in parallel.
p7-19.qa: A Promise represents a future value: pending, then fulfilled or rejected, handled with then/catch. async/await is syntax over Promises that reads like synchronous code with try/catch. Promise.all runs in parallel and fails fast; Promise.allSettled waits for all; Promise.race and Promise.any return the first to settle or succeed.
i: Unhandled rejections crash Node by default (since Node 15).
Sequential awaits in loops can be slow; use Promise.all for independent calls.
A Promise is pending, fulfilled or rejected; async/await is syntax over promises.
Promise.all for parallel work; Promise.allSettled when partial failures are fine.
f: Promise.all vs allSettled?
all rejects on the first failure; allSettled reports every result.
Is await blocking?
No, it yields to the event loop until the promise settles.

p7-20.a: Deeply nested callbacks for sequential async steps, hard to read and handle errors; solved with Promises and async/await, or by splitting into named functions.
p7-20.qa: Callback hell is deeply nested callbacks for sequential async steps, hard to read and to handle errors in; it's solved with Promises and async/await, or by splitting into named functions.
i: util.promisify converts Node callback APIs to Promises.
Error-first callbacks were the old Node convention.
Deeply nested callbacks make error handling and flow hard to follow.
Fix with promises/async-await and small named functions.
f: Why is error handling hard with callbacks?
Every level must check and pass errors manually.
Modern Node APIs?
Promise-based versions like fs/promises.

p7-21.a: Optional chaining `user?.address?.city` returns undefined instead of throwing if something is null or undefined.|Nullish coalescing `count ?? 0` uses the default only for null or undefined, unlike `||` which also replaces 0 and empty strings.
p7-21.qa: Optional chaining user?.address?.city returns undefined instead of throwing if something is null or undefined. Nullish coalescing count ?? 0 uses the default only for null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0, '' and false.
i: ??= assigns only if null/undefined.
Same operators exist in C# (?. and ??).
a?.b returns undefined instead of throwing if a is null/undefined.
x ?? y uses y only for null/undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0 and "".
f: Why ?? instead of ||?
So valid falsy values like 0 aren't replaced.
Does ?. work with function calls?
Yes, fn?.() calls only if fn exists.

p7-22.a: any turns off type checking entirely. unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow (typeof, instanceof, a type guard) before using it. Prefer unknown for untrusted data such as API responses or caught errors.
p7-22.qa: any turns off type checking entirely; unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow it (typeof, instanceof, type guards or schema validation) before use. Prefer unknown for untrusted data like API responses or caught errors.
i: catch (e) is unknown with useUnknownInCatchVariables (part of strict).
never represents impossible values (exhaustiveness checks).
any disables type checking; unknown forces you to narrow before use.
Use unknown for parsed JSON and catch variables (useUnknownInCatchVariables in strict).
f: How do you narrow unknown API data?
Validate with Zod and get typed results.
What is never used for?
Exhaustive switch checks and functions that never return.

p7-23.a: Type parameters that make code reusable while keeping types, for example `function first<T>(items: T[]): T` or `ApiResponse<Shipment>`; constraints with `extends`.
p7-23.qa: Generics are type parameters that make code reusable while keeping types, for example function first<T>(items: T[]): T or ApiResponse<Shipment>, with constraints using extends.
i: Utility types: Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, Record<K, V>.
keyof and conditional types for advanced typing.
Example: function apiGet<T>(url: string): Promise<T> gives typed API responses.
c:
async function get<T>(url: string): Promise<T> { const r = await fetch(url); return r.json() as Promise<T>; }
const shipment = await get<Shipment>('/api/shipments/42');
f: Generic constraint example?
<T extends { id: number }> ensures T has an id.
Difference from C# generics?
TypeScript generics are erased at runtime; C# generics exist at runtime.

p7-24.a: Union `A | B`: a value is one of several types, such as `'Pending' | 'Shipped'`.|Intersection `A & B`: a value has all members of both.|Narrowing: TypeScript refines a union after checks (typeof, in, discriminant property, custom type guards).
p7-24.qa: A union A | B means a value is one of several types, such as 'Pending' | 'Shipped'; an intersection A & B means a value has all members of both; narrowing is TypeScript refining a union inside checks (typeof, in, instanceof, discriminant properties).
i: Discriminated unions with a kind field give exhaustive switches.
Union: A | B (either); intersection: A & B (both).
Narrowing via typeof, in, instanceof, and discriminated unions with a kind field.
c:
type Result = { ok: true; data: Shipment } | { ok: false; error: string };
function show(r: Result) { if (r.ok) console.log(r.data.id); else console.error(r.error); }
f: What is a discriminated union?
A union whose members share a literal property used to tell them apart.
Custom type guard?
A function returning `x is Type`.

p7-25.a: In TypeScript, `strict: true` enables strict checks such as strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny, catching null and type bugs at compile time.|In JavaScript, 'use strict' (default in modules and classes) forbids sloppy features such as undeclared variables.
p7-25.qa: In TypeScript, strict: true enables strict checks such as strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny and strictFunctionTypes, catching null and type bugs at compile time. In JavaScript, 'use strict' (and ES modules automatically) turns silent errors into exceptions and forbids some unsafe features.
i: Turn on strict for new projects; migrate old ones gradually.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds safety for arrays and records.
JS "use strict" disallows silent errors (undeclared variables); ES modules are strict by default.
TypeScript "strict": true enables strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny and more.
f: What does strictNullChecks do?
Makes null and undefined separate types you must handle.
Are ES modules strict?
Yes, always.

p7-26.a: Node runs JavaScript on one thread with an event loop; asynchronous I/O lets it serve many requests while waiting. Synchronous calls (fs.readFileSync, heavy CPU loops) block every request, so use async APIs and worker threads for CPU work.
p7-26.qa: Node runs JavaScript on one thread with an event loop; asynchronous I/O (via libuv) lets it serve many requests while waiting. Synchronous calls (fs.readFileSync, heavy CPU loops) block the event loop and stall every request, so CPU-heavy work goes to worker threads or other services.
i: Event loop phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close; microtasks (Promises) run between.
libuv thread pool handles fs, DNS and crypto.
Node runs JS on a single thread with an event loop; I/O is async through libuv.
CPU-heavy sync work blocks every request; use worker threads.
f: How do you detect event loop blocking?
Event loop lag metrics (perf_hooks monitorEventLoopDelay).
Worker threads vs cluster?
Worker threads share a process for CPU tasks; cluster runs multiple processes for scaling.

p7-27.a: Express is a minimal web framework for Node.js: routing, request/response helpers and middleware.|Middleware: functions (req, res, next) that run in order for logging, auth, parsing JSON, validation and error handling; error middleware has four parameters.
p7-27.qa: Express is a minimal web framework for Node.js providing routing, request/response helpers and middleware. Middleware are functions (req, res, next) that run in order for logging, auth, parsing and error handling; error middleware has four arguments (err, req, res, next).
i: Express 5 (2024) handles rejected promises in async handlers automatically.
Same concept as ASP.NET Core middleware.
Express middleware is (req, res, next); error middleware has four args (err, req, res, next), similar to ASP.NET Core's pipeline.
c:
app.use((req, res, next) => { req.headers['x-correlation-id'] ??= randomUUID(); next(); });
app.use((err: Error, req: Request, res: Response, _next: NextFunction) => res.status(500).json({ title: 'Server error' }));
f: What happens if middleware doesn't call next?
The request hangs unless it sends a response.
Express vs Fastify?
Fastify is faster with schema-based validation; Express is simpler and more widespread.

p7-28.a: try/catch around awaited calls, a central error-handling middleware returning consistent JSON (problem details), never swallow rejections, process-level handlers for unhandledRejection to log and exit cleanly, and structured logging.
p7-28.qa: Use try/catch around awaited calls, a central error-handling middleware returning consistent JSON (problem details), never swallow rejections, add process-level handlers for unhandledRejection and uncaughtException that log and exit so the orchestrator restarts cleanly, and log with correlation ids.
i: Operational errors (expected) vs programmer errors (bugs).
Don't keep running after uncaughtException; state may be corrupt.
Express 5 forwards rejected promises from async handlers to error middleware automatically.
Handle process-level unhandledRejection to log and exit cleanly.
f: Why exit on uncaughtException?
The process may be in an unknown state; restart is safer.
How do you return errors consistently?
One error middleware mapping error types to status codes.

p7-29.a: JWT/OAuth validation middleware, input validation (Zod or Joi), helmet for security headers, rate limiting, CORS allow-list, parameterised queries, npm audit and dependency scanning, secrets from a vault, HTTPS.
p7-29.qa: JWT/OAuth validation middleware, input validation (Zod or Joi), helmet for security headers, rate limiting, a CORS allow-list, parameterised queries, npm audit and dependency scanning, secrets from a vault, and running as a non-root user in containers.
i: Lockfiles and npm ci for reproducible installs.
Supply-chain attacks on npm (e.g. compromised packages in 2025) make pinning and scanning vital.
helmet for headers, rate limiting, input validation (zod), JWT validation, and npm audit for dependencies.
Never trust req.body shapes; validate them.
f: How do you validate JWTs in Node?
Libraries like jose with JWKS from the identity provider.
What does helmet do?
Sets security headers like CSP, HSTS and X-Content-Type-Options.

p7-30.a: .NET: strong typing, high performance, great for CPU-heavy and complex domain services, mature tooling (EF Core, DI built in).|Node.js: fast for I/O-bound glue and real-time services, shares language with the frontend, huge npm ecosystem.|I use .NET for core domain services and Node for I/O-heavy helpers such as the log summariser.
p7-30.qa: .NET offers strong typing, high performance, good fit for CPU-heavy and complex domain services, and mature tooling (EF Core, built-in DI). Node.js is fast to build for I/O-bound glue and real-time work, with one language across front end and back end and a huge npm ecosystem. I choose by workload and team.
i: .NET multithreading uses all cores in one process; Node needs clustering or workers.
TypeScript narrows the type-safety gap.
Node: same language as the front end, fast for I/O-bound APIs; .NET: strong typing, high throughput, mature tooling for large systems.
Our domain services stayed .NET for performance and team skills.
f: Which for a CPU-heavy service?
.NET.
Which for a small BFF for a React app?
Node/TypeScript is a natural fit.

p7-31.a: For validation and scripting: Pydantic made vendor file schema checks quick and readable for the integration team, and Python with Shell is our release automation language alongside Ansible. Its libraries make data handling and automation fast to write.
p7-31.qa: For validation and scripting: Pydantic made vendor file schema checks quick and readable for the integration team, and Python with Shell is our release automation language alongside Ansible. Its libraries make data handling and automation fast to write.
i: [Vendor file pre-validation service] with FastAPI returns 422 with exact problems before the .NET import.
Ansible itself is Python-based.
Python was a tool for the right job, not a replacement for our .NET core services.
f: Why not do validation in .NET?
We could; Python was faster for the integration team to maintain alongside their scripts.
Python version and tools?
[Python 3.12], pytest, ruff, uv or pip-tools.
wv: I pick the right tool for the job.

p7-32.a: app/ with routers per feature, Pydantic schemas, services for business logic, a data layer, core/ for config (pydantic-settings) and security, dependencies injected with Depends, tests with pytest and TestClient, Dockerfile and uvicorn.
p7-32.qa: app/ with routers per feature, Pydantic schemas, services for business logic, a data layer, core/ for config (pydantic-settings) and security, dependencies injected with Depends, and tests with pytest and TestClient (httpx).
i: Async endpoints for I/O; run with uvicorn (or gunicorn with uvicorn workers).
Automatic OpenAPI docs at /docs.
Routers per feature, Pydantic models in schemas, dependencies via Depends, and settings with pydantic-settings.
f: What is Depends?
FastAPI's dependency injection for parameters, auth and resources.
sync vs async def?
async for non-blocking I/O; sync functions run in a thread pool.

p7-33.a: OAuth2 bearer tokens: a dependency (OAuth2PasswordBearer or HTTPBearer) extracts the JWT, validates signature, issuer, audience and expiry against the identity provider's keys, and returns the user; routes declare `user = Depends(get_current_user)` and check scopes.
p7-33.qa: OAuth2 bearer tokens: a dependency (HTTPBearer or OAuth2PasswordBearer) extracts the JWT, validates signature, issuer, audience and expiry against the identity provider's JWKS (e.g. with PyJWT), and returns the user; route dependencies check roles or scopes.
i: Cache JWKS keys; handle key rotation.
Security dependencies show in OpenAPI docs.
OAuth2PasswordBearer or HTTPBearer dependencies validating JWTs from the identity provider.
f: How do you require a role?
A dependency that checks claims and raises 403.
Why specify algorithms?
To prevent algorithm confusion attacks.

p7-34.a: SFTP: file transfer over SSH (port 22): encrypted, one connection, key or password auth.|FTP: unencrypted, separate control and data connections.|FTPS: FTP over TLS with certificates; firewall-unfriendly because of data ports.
p7-34.qa: SFTP is file transfer over SSH (port 22): encrypted, a single connection, key or password authentication. FTP is unencrypted with separate control and data connections; FTPS is FTP over TLS with certificates, still using multiple connections that complicate firewalls.
i: SFTP is not FTP over SSH; it's a different protocol (SSH File Transfer Protocol).
SCP is older and being replaced by SFTP under the hood in OpenSSH 9.
SFTP runs over SSH (port 22), one encrypted channel; FTP is plain text; FTPS is FTP over TLS with separate data channels.
SFTP is firewall-friendlier than FTPS.
f: Why do firewalls struggle with FTPS?
Encrypted control channel hides dynamic data ports from inspection.
Which do vendors prefer?
Most use SFTP with key authentication.

p7-35.a: The SSH handshake agrees algorithms and the client verifies the server's host key fingerprint (prevents man-in-the-middle); then the user authenticates.|Password: simple but can be guessed or leaked.|Private key: the client proves possession of a private key matching a public key on the server; stronger and automatable. We use keys, sometimes plus a password where vendors require both.
p7-35.qa: The SSH handshake agrees algorithms (key exchange, ciphers, MACs), and the client verifies the server's host key fingerprint to prevent man-in-the-middle; then the user authenticates. Password auth is simple but weaker; private-key auth proves possession of a key whose public part is on the server, which is stronger, automatable and preferred.
i: Pin host key fingerprints per vendor in configuration.
Modern algorithms: ed25519 or rsa-sha2-256/512 keys, curve25519 key exchange.
Protect private keys in Secrets Manager.
Key authentication: the server holds the public key, the client proves it holds the private key; no secret travels.
f: What happens if a host key changes?
Our client refuses to connect until the new fingerprint is verified and updated.
Why did ssh-rsa break?
It uses SHA-1, which servers disabled as insecure.

p7-36.a: All three providers implement ISftpClient. A factory reads the provider name per vendor from configuration (for example `Sftp:Vendors:DepotA:Provider = Rebex`) and returns the right implementation, so switching a vendor is a config change and restart, with no code change.
p7-36.qa: All three providers implement ISftpClient. A factory reads the provider name per vendor from configuration (e.g. Sftp:Vendors:DepotA:Provider = Rebex) and returns the matching implementation, so switching a vendor is a configuration change with no code deployment.
i: Options pattern with per-vendor named settings.
Keyed services (.NET 8) can replace the hand-written factory.
Rollback = flip config back.
f: Was a restart needed?
[With IOptionsMonitor, the next job picks up the change without restart].
How did you test each provider?
The same contract tests ran against all three.

p7-37.a: The base class wraps operations with Polly: [3] retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors (timeouts, connection resets), a fresh connection per attempt, no retry for auth or host key failures. After the last attempt the job is marked failed and an alert goes to the support channel; the next scheduled run picks it up again.
p7-37.qa: The base class wraps operations with Polly: [3] retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors (timeouts, connection resets), a fresh connection per attempt, and no retry for auth or host key failures. After the last attempt the job is marked failed and an alert goes to the support channel; the next scheduled run picks it up again.
i: Classify exceptions: transient vs permanent.
Polly v8 ResiliencePipeline with retry and timeout strategies.
Host key fingerprint pinning prevents man-in-the-middle; a mismatch is never retried.
f: Why not retry auth failures?
They won't fix themselves and may lock the account.
Why a fresh connection per attempt?
A broken session can't be reused safely.

p7-38.a: Compare the remote file size after upload with the local size, and where vendors support it a checksum (SHA-256) in a sidecar file.|Partial transfers: upload under a temporary name (.part), then rename when complete, so the vendor never picks up a half file; on download, read only files that are complete (stable size or a done marker) and verify before processing.

steps.title: Record
steps.detail: Log name + hash in processed table

p7-38.qa: After upload I compare the remote file size with the local size and, where vendors support it, a SHA-256 checksum in a sidecar file. For partial transfers I upload under a temporary name (.part) and rename when complete so the vendor never picks up half a file; on download I only read complete files (stable size or a done marker) and verify before processing.
i: Atomic rename is supported on most SFTP servers.
Hash computed while streaming to avoid reading twice.
Upload to a temp name then rename, so consumers never read a partial file.
Compare sizes and checksums (SHA-256 manifest) when the vendor provides them.
f: What if rename isn't allowed?
Use a separate upload folder and move, or a done marker file.
How do you detect a still-uploading vendor file?
Size stable across two checks or a marker file.

p7-39.a: Deterministic file names (vendor, type, timestamp, sequence), a processed-files table keyed by name and hash so the same file is never imported twice, and moving processed files to an archive folder.
p7-39.qa: Deterministic file names (vendor, type, timestamp, sequence), a processed-files table keyed by name and hash so the same file is never imported twice, and moving processed files to an archive folder.
i: Unique constraint on file hash.
Same file name with different content is flagged for review.
Track processed files by name plus hash in a table with a unique constraint.
Move or archive processed files on the server.
f: Why both name and hash?
Name catches re-sends; hash catches renamed duplicates.
What about reprocessing intentionally?
An audited admin action that marks the old record superseded.

p7-40.a: Private keys and passwords in [AWS Secrets Manager], read at runtime by the service role; never in config files or the repo; host key fingerprints pinned in configuration; rotation with vendors coordinated through change control; access logged.
p7-40.qa: Private keys and passwords live in [AWS Secrets Manager], read at runtime by the service's role, never in config files or the repo; host key fingerprints are pinned in configuration; keys are rotated with vendors on a schedule; and access is logged.
i: Separate credentials per vendor and environment.
Keys never written to disk; loaded into memory streams.
Keys and passwords in AWS Secrets Manager, read at runtime via the task role.
Rotation with vendors coordinated through change control.
f: How do you rotate keys with vendors?
Add the new public key on their side, switch, then remove the old one.
Who can read the secrets?
Only the service role and a small ops group, audited via CloudTrail.

p7-41.a: Situation: vendor servers differ.|Task: keep transfers reliable.|Action and examples: [a depot vendor disabled ssh-rsa with SHA-1], which broke ComponentPro and led us to Rebex; [a vendor moved their pickup folder] without telling our team, so we added post-upload checks and alerts; [timeouts on large files over slow links], fixed with longer operation timeouts and resumable uploads.|Result: [no failed transfers caused by the switch], and faster diagnosis when vendors change things.
p7-41.qa: Vendor servers differ, so I kept transfers reliable through several problems: [a depot vendor disabled ssh-rsa with SHA-1], which broke ComponentPro and led us to Rebex; [a vendor moved their pickup folder] without telling our team, so we added post-upload checks and alerts; and [timeouts on large files over slow links], fixed with longer operation timeouts and resumable uploads. No failed transfers were caused by the switch, and diagnosis got faster.
i: Pattern: abstraction plus observability plus communication.
Per-vendor configuration for algorithms, timeouts and paths.
Vendor server quirks: different directory listing formats, timeouts, and files still being written.
f: Most annoying issue?
Silent vendor changes; fixed with verification and a shared contact list.
What would you add next?
Synthetic daily test transfers per vendor.
wv: I handle messy real-world integrations patiently and systematically.

p7-42.a: Unit tests with a mocked ISftpClient for the business flow; integration tests against a containerised OpenSSH test server in CI (upload, download, list, rename, wrong key, bad host key, timeouts, a large file); contract checks against each vendor's test endpoint before go-live.
p7-42.qa: Unit tests with a mocked ISftpClient for the business flow; integration tests against a containerised OpenSSH test server in CI (upload, download, list, rename, wrong key, wrong host key, timeouts, large files); and vendor test endpoints before production.
i: Testcontainers with atmoz/sftp image.
Contract tests run against every provider.
Testcontainers with an atmoz/sftp container for integration tests plus fakes for unit tests.
f: How do you test host key mismatch?
Configure a wrong fingerprint and assert the connection is refused.
Why vendor test endpoints too?
Real servers have quirks a test container doesn't.

p7-43.a: WCF: .NET Framework framework for SOAP services over many transports (HTTP, TCP, named pipes) with WS-* security and transactions; heavy configuration.|Web API: lightweight HTTP/REST with JSON, cross-platform on ASP.NET Core, easy for browsers and mobile. New work uses Web API or gRPC; CoreWCF exists for migrations.
p7-43.qa: WCF is a .NET Framework framework for SOAP services over many transports (HTTP, TCP, named pipes, MSMQ) with WS-* security, reliable messaging and transactions, but heavy configuration. Web API (ASP.NET Core) is lightweight HTTP/REST with JSON, cross-platform and the modern standard; gRPC is the recommended replacement for WCF's binary, contract-first scenarios.
i: WCF server isn't part of modern .NET; CoreWCF is a community port for migration.
WCF clients (System.ServiceModel packages) work on modern .NET.
WCF supports SOAP, multiple transports and WS-* standards; Web API is HTTP/REST and JSON-first.
WCF server isn't in modern .NET; CoreWCF is the community port.
f: What replaces NetTcpBinding?
gRPC for high-performance contract-based calls.
What is CoreWCF?
An open-source port of WCF server to modern .NET, supported by Microsoft for migrations.

p7-44.a: Simple Object Access Protocol: an XML messaging protocol with an envelope, header and body, described by a WSDL contract, supporting WS-Security and reliable messaging.
p7-44.qa: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) is an XML messaging protocol with an envelope, header and body, described by a WSDL contract, supporting standards like WS-Security and reliable messaging. It's strict and verbose but still common in enterprise and healthcare integrations.
i: SOAP faults for errors.
Tools generate clients from WSDL (dotnet-svcutil).
XML envelope protocol with WSDL contracts; strongly typed but verbose.
Still common in older enterprise and healthcare integrations.
f: SOAP vs REST?
SOAP is a protocol with strict contracts; REST is an architectural style using HTTP semantics.
How do you call SOAP from .NET 8?
Generate a client with dotnet-svcutil or Connected Services.

p7-45.a: [ServiceContract]: marks an interface as a WCF service.|[OperationContract]: marks a method in it as an exposed operation.|[DataContract] and [DataMember]: mark classes and properties that are serialised in messages.
p7-45.qa: [ServiceContract] marks an interface as a WCF service; [OperationContract] marks a method in it as an exposed operation; [DataContract] and [DataMember] mark classes and properties to serialize with the DataContractSerializer. Together they define the WSDL contract.
i: [FaultContract] declares typed faults.
Versioning by adding optional DataMembers (IsRequired=false).
[ServiceContract] marks an interface, [OperationContract] its methods, [DataContract]/[DataMember] the payloads.
They define the WSDL that clients generate proxies from.
f: What is DataContractSerializer?
WCF's opt-in XML serializer for data contracts.
Equivalent in gRPC?
Service and message definitions in .proto files.

p7-46.a: There is no built-in container in classic .NET Framework apps, so teams used Unity, Autofac, Ninject or Castle Windsor, wiring them into WCF with a custom instance provider or into MVC with a dependency resolver. ASP.NET Core made DI built in.
p7-46.qa: Classic .NET Framework apps have no built-in container, so teams used Unity, Autofac, Ninject or Castle Windsor, wiring them into WCF with a custom instance provider or service host factory (and into MVC/Web API with dependency resolvers). Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection can also be used in .NET Framework.
i: Composition root at application start (Global.asax).
Autofac has WCF integration packages.
No built-in container in .NET Framework; teams used Unity, Autofac or Ninject.
WCF needed custom IInstanceProvider to inject services.
f: Can you use MS DI in .NET Framework?
Yes, the package targets .NET Standard.
Why was DI harder in WCF?
WCF creates service instances itself, so you must hook its instance creation.

p7-47.a: Why: WCF server is not in modern .NET, Windows/IIS-bound, heavy configuration, and clients prefer REST/JSON; moving to .NET 8+ gives performance, containers and support.|Challenges: existing SOAP clients that cannot change (use CoreWCF or a facade), WS-* security and transactions, contract compatibility, testing every operation, and running old and new side by side during cut-over.
p7-47.qa: Why migrate: WCF server isn't in modern .NET, it's Windows/IIS-bound with heavy configuration, and clients prefer REST/JSON; moving to .NET 8/10 gives performance, containers and support. Challenges: SOAP clients that can't change, WS-* features (security, transactions), duplex callbacks, binary bindings, and behaviour differences, so migrate incrementally (CoreWCF, a facade, or strangler pattern).
i: Contract tests to ensure compatibility.
Keep a SOAP facade while moving logic to new services.
Reasons: no WCF server in modern .NET, tooling and hosting limits, and the team's skills moving to REST.
Challenges: SOAP clients still needing contracts, WS-Security, and testing parity.
f: What's the safest approach?
Strangler fig: route operations to new services gradually.
Duplex replacement?
SignalR or gRPC streaming.

p7-48.a: Interactive Response Technology: the system clinical trials use to randomise patients to treatment arms and manage drug supply, kit dispensing and shipments to sites (also called RTSM).
p7-48.qa: IRT means Interactive Response Technology: the system clinical trials use to randomise patients to treatment arms and manage drug supply, kit dispensing and shipments to sites. It was historically IVRS/IWRS (voice and web response systems), also called RTSM (Randomization and Trial Supply Management).
i: Core functions: subject registration, randomization, dispensing, resupply, unblinding, reporting.
Integrations with EDC, depots, couriers.
Blinding: sites and patients don't know which arm; IRT controls kit assignment to keep it.
That's why audit and access controls are strict.
f: What is RTSM?
Randomization and Trial Supply Management, another name for IRT.
What is unblinding?
Revealing a subject's treatment, controlled and audited, e.g. for emergencies.

p7-49.a: GxP: 'good practice' regulations (GCP, GMP, GLP) and related rules such as FDA 21 CFR Part 11 for electronic records.|Important because patient safety and trial data integrity depend on the software being correct, controlled and auditable; failures can invalidate trial data or harm patients.
p7-49.qa: GxP refers to "good practice" regulations (GCP, GMP, GLP and more) and related rules such as FDA 21 CFR Part 11 for electronic records and signatures and EU Annex 11. It matters because patient safety and trial data integrity depend on systems behaving correctly, and regulators can reject trial data or take action if systems aren't validated.
i: GAMP 5 guides risk-based validation of computerised systems.

Computer Software Assurance (FDA final guidance Sept 2025, updated Feb 2026) is written for medical-device production and quality systems, but its risk-based, less documentation-heavy testing approach is widely borrowed across GxP.
GxP: Good x Practice (clinical, manufacturing, laboratory) regulations ensuring product quality and patient safety.
For software: 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11 for electronic records and signatures.
f: What is 21 CFR Part 11?
FDA rules for trustworthy electronic records and signatures.
What is GAMP 5?
Industry guidance for risk-based validation of computerised systems.

p7-50.a: Documented requirements traced to tests, formal validation (FV) and UAT with evidence, change control for every release, code review and approvals, audit trails, access control, and no direct production changes. It slows releases but makes them predictable.
p7-50.qa: GxP means documented requirements traced to tests, formal validation (FV) and UAT with evidence, change control for every release, code review and approvals, audit trails, access controls and separation of duties, and controlled deployments; development is slower but more predictable and safe.
i: Risk-based testing focuses effort on high-impact functions.
Automation must itself be controlled (pipelines as code, validated tools).
Documented requirements, risk-based validation, traceability to tests, and controlled changes.
CSA guidance (FDA final Sept 2025) promotes risk-based, less documentation-heavy assurance.
f: Does GxP prevent agile?
No, agile works with validation built into the definition of done.
Who signs off?
QA/validation and business owners.

p7-51.a: Validation: documented evidence that the system does what it is intended to do, consistently.|Traceability: links from requirement to design, code, test and release.|Auditability: every create, change and delete is recorded with who, when, what and why, and cannot be altered.
p7-51.qa: Validation is documented evidence that the system does what it's intended to do, consistently; traceability links requirements to design, code, tests and releases; auditability means every change and action can be reconstructed (who, what, when, why) from records.
i: Traceability matrix maps requirements to test cases and results.
Azure DevOps links work items, commits, builds and releases.
Validation proves software does what it should; traceability links requirements to tests.
Auditability: who did what, when, and why, recorded in tamper-evident audit trails.
f: How do you prove traceability?
A matrix and tool links from requirement to test evidence and release.
What breaks auditability?
Manual undocumented changes or shared accounts.

p7-52.a: A formal process where every change to a validated system is requested, assessed for impact and risk, approved, tested, documented and released in a controlled way, with rollback plans.
p7-52.qa: Change control is a formal process where every change to a validated system is requested, assessed for impact and risk, approved, tested, documented and released in a controlled way, with the ability to roll back. Emergency changes follow an expedited but still documented path.
i: Change request includes scope, risk, test plan, rollback plan, approvals.
Post-implementation review.
Every change has a request, risk assessment, approvals, testing evidence and a release record.
Emergency changes still get documented afterwards.
f: What's an emergency change?
An urgent fix with expedited approval and documentation completed promptly.
How do you speed up change control?
Small changes, automation of evidence and standard pre-approved change types.

p7-53.a: FV (formal validation): the validation team executes scripted tests against requirements and records evidence.|TechOps: the operations team that installs and verifies releases in controlled environments and production.|UAT (user acceptance testing): business users or the client confirm the release meets their needs before production.
p7-53.qa: FV (formal validation) is the validation team executing scripted tests against requirements and recording evidence; TechOps is the operations team that installs and verifies releases in controlled environments; UAT is user acceptance testing where business users confirm the release meets their needs before production.
i: Order: FV, TechOps, UAT, production in our pipeline.
Defects found lead to fixes and re-validation.
UAT: users accept functionality; FV: functional validation by QA; TechOps: production operations.
Each gates promotion to the next environment.
f: Who runs UAT?
Business users or their representatives with test scripts.
What do you provide to FV?
Release notes, test data, known issues and support during execution.

p7-54.a: Only approved, versioned artifacts from the pipeline; change requests with approvals; deployment by TechOps or the controlled pipeline, never manual edits; separation of duties; verification after deployment; everything logged.
p7-54.qa: Only approved, versioned artifacts from the pipeline go to production; change requests with approvals; deployment by TechOps or the controlled pipeline, never manual edits; separation of duties; audit logs; and post-deployment verification.
i: Read-only production access for developers; break-glass access audited.
Configuration changes follow the same process.
Approved change requests, gated pipelines and segregated access to production.
Our MCP release tools kept human approvals and logged every action.
f: Can developers access production?
Read-only logs and metrics; changes only through the process.
What is break-glass access?
Emergency elevated access with approval, time limits and audit.

p7-55.a: Automated tests (unit, integration, Playwright E2E), SonarQube quality gates, mandatory reviews, definition of done that includes validation documents, FV and UAT, root-cause analysis for defects, and small, well-understood changes.
p7-55.qa: Automated tests (unit, integration, Playwright end-to-end), SonarQube quality gates, mandatory reviews, a definition of done including validation documents, FV and UAT, root-cause analysis with CAPA for defects, and continuous improvement from retrospectives.
i: Shift-left: test and review early.
Metrics: escaped defects, change failure rate.
Automated tests and code reviews, plus validation documentation for traceability.
Static analysis and dependency scanning in CI.
f: What's CAPA?
Corrective and Preventive Action after an issue.
How do you avoid slowing down?
Automate tests and evidence collection.

p7-56.a: SSO with role-based access and least privilege, blinding protection (who may see treatment assignments), encryption in transit and at rest, audit trails, secure coding and scans, protection of PHI and patient data, regular penetration tests and fast patching.
p7-56.qa: SSO with role-based access and least privilege, blinding protection (only authorised roles see treatment assignments), encryption in transit and at rest, audit trails, secure coding and OWASP checks, vulnerability scanning, privacy rules for patient data (GDPR, HIPAA), and regular security reviews and penetration tests.
i: Pseudonymised subject identifiers; minimal PHI.
Security fixes: logout, SSO cookie, tabnabbing (Part 3 Q19).
Role-based access, encryption in transit and at rest, audit trails, and blinding-safe data exposure.
Pen testing and OWASP checks; our tabnabbing fix across [~40] links is one example.
f: Why is blinding a security issue?
Leaking treatment assignments could bias trial results.
How do you protect patient data in logs?
Never log PHI; redact and review log templates.

p7-57.a: IRT creates shipment orders and sends them to depot and courier vendors via SFTP files or APIs; vendors return status files or webhooks (dispatched, in transit, delivered, temperature excursion); IRT validates, updates shipment status, raises events (Kafka/RabbitMQ) and notifies sites.
p7-57.qa: IRT creates shipment orders and sends them to depot and courier vendors via SFTP files or APIs; vendors return status files or webhooks (dispatched, in transit, delivered); our integration services validate, deduplicate and process them idempotently, publish events to update shipments and notify sites, and alert on failures or delays.
i: [SFTP poller every 5 minutes] for status files.
Kafka events for shipment status consumed by several services.
Reconciliation reports catch missed updates.
Message contracts are versioned so vendors can change formats without breaking us.
f: How do you handle out-of-order statuses?
Compare status timestamps and ignore older updates.
What if a vendor sends a bad file?
Pre-validation rejects it with exact errors and alerts the integration team.

p7-58.a: Depot and courier vendors (SFTP files and APIs for shipments), EDC and clinical systems (subject data), SSO identity provider, email and notification services, and sponsor reporting exports. Each has validation, retries, monitoring and audit.
p7-58.qa: Depot and courier vendors (SFTP files and APIs for shipments), EDC and clinical systems (subject data), the SSO identity provider, email and notification services, and sponsor reporting and data exports.
i: Each integration has contracts, monitoring and runbooks.
Anti-corruption layers translate external models.
Depots and couriers (SFTP/APIs), EDC systems, identity providers (SSO), and notification services.
Each integration has monitoring and reconciliation.
f: Most fragile integration?
Vendor file exchanges, because vendors change things independently.
How do you monitor integrations?
Success/failure metrics per vendor, alerts and reconciliation.

p7-59.a: ALCOA+ principles (attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate); database constraints and transactions; validation at the API; immutable audit trails; idempotent processing; backups; reconciliation reports with vendors; restricted direct database access.
p7-59.qa: ALCOA+ principles (attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring, available); database constraints and transactions; validation at the API; immutable audit trails; idempotent processing; backups with tested restores; and reconciliation between systems.
i: UTC timestamps from synchronised clocks for contemporaneous records.
No shared accounts so actions are attributable.
Database constraints, transactions, idempotency keys and validation at every boundary.
Audit trails and reconciliation reports confirm nothing was lost or altered.
f: What does attributable mean?
Every record shows who created or changed it.
How do you detect integrity problems?
Reconciliation jobs and constraint violations alerts.
